note: Hand-written rest-stop scenes for the director's own Delta Pokémon (drive) and for species the pack has no lore for (lore). Read by core/overhaul/partyNarration.ts.

entries.scene: The bulb hums faintly at night, and glowing spores drift up like tiny lanterns.
Its tail flame burns a cold, pale colour, and it keeps checking that you can still feel the warmth.
It taps its shell twice, a little signal, and waits for you to tap back.
It stands very still, listening to something far away, then smiles at you as if it heard your name.
It polishes its blades against a stone, slow and careful, like a swordsman before a promise.
It circles the camp once, twice, then lands on your shoulder as though it had always belonged there.
It coils into a small, tight spiral and falls asleep, one eye always a little open for you.
Sparks crackle along its cheeks in colours no Pikachu should have, and it looks pleased about it.
It sleeps through the whole rest stop, and somehow the camp feels safer for it.
It rolls a pebble over to you, then looks away, pretending it was nothing.
It sits at the edge of the firelight, guarding the dark so everyone else can rest.
It huffs a few shy embers, then curls up against your boot to keep them lit.
It watches the trees move in the wind and sways with them, perfectly in time.
It scratches a small circle in the dirt and stands in the middle of it, very proud.
A tiny seedling on its shell has bloomed overnight, and it will not stop showing you.
It stretches out on a sunny rock with an air of royalty and expects you to notice.
It skips stones across a puddle and counts the ripples under its breath.
Its fur lifts with static whenever you come close, and it leans in to make it worse.
It hangs upside down from a branch and chirps at the moon until the moon, somehow, answers.
It hides among the stumps, then peeks out to see whether you were really looking.
It breathes on the window glass and draws a tiny face in the frost.
It drifts a polite distance away so its smoke won't bother you, and then drifts back.
It leaves a trail of glittering ooze and looks back, worried you might be upset.
It splashes into the nearest puddle, utterly delighted, and invites everyone along.
It guards the snack bag with a stare that says it will not be moved.
It giggles from behind a tree, vanishes, and giggles from behind another.
It tries to become you, gets the hair wrong, and looks heartbroken until you laugh.
It lies still in the shallows, ancient and patient, and clicks once when you pass.
It stays awake for the whole night watch and nods very seriously at every sound.
It bobs along above the party, tugging gently at the sleeve of whoever looks lonely.
It twirls its antennae until the air smells of rain, then waits for applause.
It coughs a little smoke and warms your hands without being asked.
It floats on a leaf in the nearest stream and sails slowly in circles, content.
It stands guard at the camp entrance, bladed and solemn, though it keeps glancing back at you.
It cools the water bottles with a proud little shiver.
It follows the sunlight around the camp, always a few steps behind and entirely happy.
It returns the thing it borrowed from you, but only after a long, meaningful look.
It glows softly in the dusk, a lantern in the shape of a jellyfish.
It pops up from the ground right at your feet, then ducks away giggling.
Its two heads argue about the best spot to sleep, then fall asleep mid-sentence.
It puffs up its chest on a fence post and keeps lookout like it has a very important job.
It nibbles a crumb with great ceremony and tucks the rest away for later.
It coils around a warm rock and tastes the air, learning everything about the night.
It curls into a ball and rolls down a little slope, over and over, for the pure joy of it.
Only its head shows above the ground, and it seems to be listening to the earth.
It shadow-boxes a tree until it is out of breath, then looks around to see who watched.
It sways to a tune only it can hear and tries to get a leaf to dance along.
It drifts in a rain puddle that is far too small for it and seems content anyway.
It tucks itself into its shell and is not seen again until someone mentions berries.
It swings from a low branch by its tail, showing off until someone claps.
It floats in a puddle with its leaf-hat tilted, enjoying the rain on its back.
It hangs from a branch like an acorn and drops, now and then, to scare a friend.
It dives to catch a tossed berry, snaps it out of the air, and puffs up proudly.
It rides the breeze above the camp, sliding on the wind without a single flap.
It skates across a pond so lightly that the water barely ripples.
It sits very still in the shade, convinced no one has seen it.
It has not moved since the last stop, and it is somehow still tired.
It clings to a tree trunk and listens, as if the bark were whispering.
It takes a very deep breath, thinks better of it, and whispers instead.
It practises its push-ups at dawn, sweating and cheerful, and counts out loud.
It bounces on its tail like a ball, giggling, and tumbles into your lap.
It sits cross-legged on a boulder, eyes closed, and the camp falls quiet around it.
It races a circle around the camp until its fur crackles, then flops down, grinning.
It sits as still as a stone, then slowly warms until the stones around it steam.
It bounces in place, trying to keep its pearl balanced, and wobbles when you look.
It digs a small pit and waits at the bottom, patient as sand.
It keeps its distance but leaves a flower on your pack when it thinks you aren't looking.
It rests on your hat like a cloud and hums a tune you can't quite place.
It sharpens its claws and glares into the dark, ready for an old rival that never comes.
It watches from the rocks, tail curled like a blade, waiting for a rival who never shows.
It wriggles in the mud and flicks it at your boots, then pretends it was the wind.
It clacks its claws in a rhythm, daring the world to keep time.
It spins on one foot all through the night, humming an ancient tune.
It hides at the bottom of the pond, and for a moment you see a shimmer of something wonderful.
It floats at the edge of the firelight, staring at nothing, then glances at you kindly.
It rolls from one side of the camp to the other, clapping its flippers all the way.
It stares up at the sky, headbutts a rock, and dreams out loud about flying.
It hovers beside you, magnetic and silent, an ancient steel thought waiting to grow.
It trills at dawn so loudly that the whole camp wakes, and it looks delighted with itself.
It gnaws a log with great purpose and the log is gone by morning.
It plays its little song for the dusk and waits for the crickets to answer.
It floats on its back in the stream, tail whirling, like a boat with no hurry.
It drinks the morning dew and glows a little redder than before.
It chews a branch in half, looks at the splinters, and looks very sorry.
It senses your mood from across the camp and quietly sits close.
It dozes in the sand, sprays a lazy fountain, and wakes up for nothing.
It croaks a warning at the dark, then squints to see if the dark is impressed.
It sits in a patch of snow it brought along and blinks, perfectly at home.
It buzzes between the camp lantern and the radio, delighted by everything with a wire.
Its flame flickers in time with your thoughts, and it leans closer to hear them.
